question: A 50-year-old female presents to her physician with vesicles and tense blisters across her chest, arms, and the back of her shoulders. Physical examination reveals that blistering is not present in her oral mucosa, and the epidermis does not separate upon light stroking of the skin. The patient most likely suffers from a hypersensitivity reaction located:?

options.opa: Linearly along the epidermal basement membrane
options.opb: In net-like patterns around epidermal cells
options.opc: In granular deposits at the tips of dermal papillae
options.opd: In fat cells beneath the skin

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Vesicles and tense blisters" -> "No oral mucosa involvement" -> "Negative Nikolsky sign" -> "Subepidermal blistering" -> "Linear IgG deposition" -> "Epidermal basement membrane" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Vesicles and tense blisters" -> "No oral mucosa involvement" -> "Negative Nikolsky sign" -> "Subepidermal blistering" -> "Granular IgA deposition" -> "Dermal papillae" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Vesicles and tense blisters" -> "No oral mucosa involvement" -> "Negative Nikolsky sign" -> "Subepidermal blistering" -> "Linear IgG deposition" -> "Linearly along the epidermal basement membrane" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Vesicles and tense blisters" -> "No oral mucosa involvement" -> "Negative Nikolsky sign" -> "Subepidermal blistering" -> "Possible IgA deposition" -> "Granular deposits at the tips of dermal papillae" -> 60%
analysis: The clinical presentation of vesicles and tense blisters, particularly without oral mucosa involvement and negative Nikolsky sign (epidermis does not separate upon light stroking), is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid. This condition is associated with autoantibodies against components of the hemidesmosomes, leading to a linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the epidermal basement membrane.
